title: Security Track Intro — Randall Degges, Snyk
talk_summary: This is a two-minute conference track introduction by Randall Degges of Snyk, not a technical talk. He frames three barriers to shipping AI-built software at scale: AI-generated code can contain security flaws, autonomous agents in production may go off the rails, and geopolitics restricts model access; then he advertises the security track sessions.

takeaways.technique: Treat agent-generated code as a normal source of security defects in the SDLC
takeaways.what_they_do: Argues that because AI models, like humans, produce security issues, security review must be a standard part of the development lifecycle rather than a special case for AI code.
takeaways.evidence_quote: when humans write code, we generate security issues. When AI models write code, turns out they also generate security issues

takeaways.technique: Explicit guardrails for autonomous agents in production
takeaways.what_they_do: Names the core problem as deploying autonomous agents such that you can 'go to sleep easily' without them doing unintended harm, implying scoped permissions and containment are required.
takeaways.evidence_quote: how do you do that in a way that allows you to go to sleep easily and not worry that the agents you deployed are going to go off the rails

takeaways.what_they_do: Notes that loss of access to specific models (e.g., 'Fable', GPT-5.6) is a real operational risk, framing provider dependency as a security/continuity concern.
takeaways.evidence_quote: how many people were kind of annoyed when access to Fable got pulled
